8.0.0.en: After the killing of Stephen there began a severe persecution of the Christians of Jerusalem, with imprisonment, plunder and flogging of the believers, but God turned it to good, for the believers were scattered throughout all the villages of Judea and Samaria, that is, the southern and middle parts of the country. They chose Samaria because its people were naturally at enmity with the Jews, so they could not hand over the fleeing Christians to the Jews of Jerusalem. As for the Apostles, they would not leave Jerusalem, and stood firm to prove the steadfastness of the faith of the newborn Church.

8.1.0.en: Some devout Jewish men came and carried the body of Stephen, and made great lamentation over him to declare their displeasure at his killing, for they felt that he was righteous and did not deserve death, although they did not yet believe in the Christian faith.

8.1.1.en: The Christians were keeping away and hiding because of the Jewish persecution rising against them.

8.2.0.en: As for Saul: he was a Jew, whose name in Latin means "the important one," of the tribe of Benjamin, from the city of Tarsus, born at the beginning of the first Christian century, so that his age was then about forty years. He had studied in the famous school of Tarsus, like the school of Alexandria and the school of Athens. Saul was consenting to the persecution of the Christians that was going on, and took part in it by raiding the Church to steal what was in it and what the believers had of money, and he seized them and imprisoned them.

8.3.1.en: As for the Christians who were scattered from Jerusalem, in their wanderings they were not afraid of the Jews but were preaching the word despite the persecution that had befallen them.

8.4.0.en: Philip the deacon, one of the companions of the martyr Stephen, came down from Jerusalem, which is raised high on the mountains, to the land of Samaria, which is the middle part of the land of the Jews, and began to preach Christ to them.

8.5.0.en: There was an intense and collective response to his preaching, for they remembered Christ's preaching among them and His meeting with the Samaritan woman about 7 years before. They were impressed by the words of the preaching and amazed at the signs that accompanied it, such as the evil spirits coming out of those possessed by them, the spirits crying out with a great, terrifying voice at the power of the name of Christ. Many who were palsied (paralyzed) and lame were also healed.

8.6.0.en: Joy came to the city through the new faith and the great healing miracles.

8.6.1.en: Truly the Lord turns sorrow into joy and spiritual gain, and controls all the events of life to work for our salvation as long as we love Him (Rom 8:28). So do not be disturbed by afflictions, for God turns them to your good.

8.7.0.en: Simon the sorcerer lived in the town of Samaria, and he was the head of a heresy that spread afterward, called "al-Tursisiyyah," in which he claimed that he was the Son of God and that he was the Holy Spirit, and the Samaritans were amazed at his satanic miracles.

8.8.0.en: All followed him as a great man, thinking that he did this because he represented the power of God, and since he had had a long time, he succeeded in drawing many.

8.9.0.en: The things concerning the Kingdom of God: the reign of God over hearts, and His work in the believers within His Church through the Holy Sacraments.

8.9.1.en: The name of Jesus Christ: faith in Christ the Redeemer.

8.9.2.en: The preaching of Philip the deacon about Christ and the Kingdom of God made them believe in God and be baptized. Thus the Church of Samaria was founded, which was later known by the name of the Church of "Sebastia," from which came the Forty Martyrs mentioned in the Synaxarium and the Synod.

8.10.0.en: Simon then believed with a false faith, seeking benefit from the new situation, to get the chance to enter the Church and fight it from within after learning how to work miracles, thinking that the Apostles were sorcerers like himself. For this reason he stayed close to Philip and was astonished that he could not learn the making of the miracles, which he thought to be a kind of sorcery. His wickedness appeared afterward (vv. 18-23).

8.11.0.en: The response of the Apostles in Jerusalem to the news of the founding of the Church of Samaria was to send two close friends, Peter and John, who went down from Jerusalem, built on the mountains, to Samaria in the north to declare the Church's acceptance of the Samaritans into her fellowship, and the rejection of the Jewish fanaticism that forbids mingling with the Samaritans, and also to support the preaching in Samaria, and so that they might complete the grace for the believers by granting them the Holy Spirit. So they prayed with their apostolic authority for the descent of the Holy Spirit on the new believers. Here we see the greatness of the sacrament of the priesthood, for it is the right of the bishops, like the Apostles, to bestow the Holy Spirit on the baptized, by laying their hands on the baptized or by the priests anointing them with the oil of the Holy Myron.

8.12.0.en: Because of the small number of bishops and priests in the apostolic age, deacons such as Philip were permitted to baptize, but they have no authority to give the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Myron. So when Peter and John came, they prayed and laid their hands on the baptized and they received the Holy Spirit, that is, the sacrament of the Myron. Note here that the laying on of hands, which the Church received from the Church of the Old Testament, was a churchly delivery to show the authority of the priesthood.

8.13.0.en: The power: that is, the giving of the Holy Spirit, which was the right of the Apostles, so that if Simon were given the Holy Spirit, including the working of miracles, he would have a greater standing in the eyes of the people. Simon thought that the transfer of this authority to him was possible by bribery and paying the right price, so he offered a sum of money to the two Apostles, asking for this authority.

8.14.0.en: The Apostle Peter was angry and refused Simon's money, because the Holy Spirit does not come in return for a sum of money, and this thinking leads to destruction.

8.15.0.en: You have neither part: you will not receive the descent of the Holy Spirit or His gifts.

8.15.1.en: This matter: that is, the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him.

8.15.2.en: Not right: you do not believe in Christ out of love for Him and do not want to walk a spiritual walk, but you are still attached to money and position and want to use Christianity and the work of the Holy Spirit to achieve your purposes. Peter recalled, as a Jew, what Joshua did when he distributed the portions of the Promised Land among the tribes of old, so he declared to Simon that the crookedness of his heart had removed from him his share in the promise of the New Testament and the inheritance of the Kingdom, so his Christianity is rejected.

8.16.0.en: The bond of this: bribery to acquire the gifts of God with money.

8.16.1.en: Pray God: prayer is accepted from the repentant, so repentance is necessary first. If perhaps: if your repentance is sincere, you receive forgiveness, otherwise you will not receive it.

8.16.2.en: Peter called Simon to repent of this perverse thought and to pray to God, who could forgive him if his repentance was sincere.

8.17.0.en: The gall of bitterness: it means the severity of the sin into which Simon had fallen, which makes his life very bitter.

8.17.1.en: The bond of iniquity: a figure of his slavery to sin, by which he wrongs himself and leads others astray and wrongs them.

8.17.2.en: Pray ye: Simon was afraid at the words of the two Apostles, and even felt that his prayer was not accepted as a result of his falling into sin, so he asked for their prayer on his behalf, and this means two things:

8.17.3.en: 1- His heart was not moved by repentance and love of God.

8.17.4.en: 2- The importance of intercession in the prayers of others for them.

8.17.5.en: None of these things which ye have spoken: the destruction and eternal torment that the two Apostles warned him against reaching as a result of his wickedness.

8.18.0.en: Testified and preached: they completed the preaching and teaching of the Christian faith and the details of worship and spiritual conduct.

8.18.1.en: Preached in many villages: the ministry of the two Apostles was not limited to the city of Samaria, but they preached in many villages of the Samaritans, and this shows the importance of serving rich and poor, and also shows concern for every person. The two Apostles returned to Jerusalem, preaching in the villages on their way back.

8.18.2.en: Among the most dangerous things is trafficking in religion, a man's seeking religiosity not out of love for God but to gain a private benefit, the thing into which Judas fell when he finally sold his Master, and as Simon did, so that everyone who traffics in religion is called a simoniac.

8.18.3.en: Examine yourself, my brother: do you come to church and serve God out of love for Him, or do you have other purposes???

8.18.4.en: Do not lose your eternity for the sake of passing material things.

8.19.s.en: (3) Philip the deacon and the eunuch

8.19.0.en: Down: because Jerusalem is built on the mountain.

8.19.1.en: Which is desert: that is, the desert road surrounded by wilderness.

8.19.2.en: God inspired an angel to speak to Philip and call him to go south to the desert road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza, which is about a hundred kilometers long, running from Jerusalem westward to the Palestinian city of Gaza.

8.20.0.en: When Philip obeyed and went south and then west, he found an Ethiopian man, a proselyte to Judaism, who was a minister of the queen of Ethiopia, who was entitled Candace, a title like "Pharaoh" in Egypt and not a name, and he was in charge of the treasuries of the kingdom. We note that Solomon the Wise had a relation with Ethiopia since the queen of Sheba visited him. From that time there was a large Jewish community in Ethiopia, as there was in Alexandria.

8.21.0.en: After performing worship in Jerusalem, the eunuch was returning to his country, riding in his chariot and reading the Book of Isaiah, and this shows his devotion in his care to read the Holy Scriptures and not any trivial readings or yielding to laziness and ease.

8.22.0.en: Go near: walk beside the chariot.

8.22.1.en: Ran thither to him: he greeted the eunuch and spoke with him as a traveler on the same road, but on foot.

8.22.2.en: The Holy Spirit asked Philip to go forward to meet the minister, and this confirms for us the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, for He is a hypostasis and not merely the power of God in the general sense.

8.23.0.en: Ran: Philip began the conversation with the eunuch.

8.23.1.en: Heard him read: the eunuch was reading aloud, and this helps many to concentrate on what they read.

8.23.2.en: He desired Philip: it appeared from Philip's words that he understood the words of Isaiah, so the eunuch seized the opportunity and asked him to ride with him and explain to him.

8.23.3.en: Philip asked him how well he understood what he was reading, and the man answered with great humility, asking for guidance and help, and invited Philip to get in and sit with him.

8.24.0.en: Opened not his mouth: Christ gave His life Himself for the redemption of mankind, so He did not defend Himself against the charges directed at Him, like sheep led to the slaughter, silent.

8.24.1.en: In his humiliation: He bore in humility all the sufferings, insults and injustice.

8.24.2.en: His judgment was taken away: the chief priests obtained an unjust sentence against Christ from the judging authority, that is, Pilate.

8.24.3.en: His generation: those contemporary with Christ.

8.24.4.en: Who shall declare: none of His contemporaries understands that He suffers for mankind and not for an evil He has done. His life is taken: He is sentenced to death on earth, but He is alive as God, so He rises again.

8.24.5.en: The eunuch was reading in Isaiah (Isa 53:7, 8), where he describes a person led to death while silent like a sheep or ewe at its slaughter or shearing, who in humility bore an unjust sentence that the wicked took from the judging authority, and killed Him. And the Jews of His generation did not understand that He suffered and died for others and not for a fault He had committed.

8.24.6.en: Then the eunuch asked Philip for the interpretation of these verses, and about the person of whom they speak... is it Isaiah or someone else?

8.25.0.en: Philip began to explain to the eunuch the story of the life of Christ and His redemption, and how these verses apply to Him, and how the Church began, and the joining of the believers by Baptism and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon them.

8.26.0.en: When they came to a pool of water, the eunuch asked Philip whether there was anything to prevent his being baptized. This confirms two things:

8.26.1.en: The first: that Baptism was performed only with much water, that is, by immersion, for if it were done by sprinkling he would have used the water he had with him, since a traveler in the desert must have drinking water with him. The second thing is that Philip spoke to him about Baptism and its importance after the acceptance of the faith.

8.27.0.en: I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God: he declared a brief faith in Christ the Savior and in His divinity. Philip made sure of the minister's faith in order to fulfill the Lord's commandment that "he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved" (Mk 16:16). This of course applies to adults, but as for children, their Christian parents can answer for them in the confession of faith until they grow up, so that they do not lose the blessing of the renewal of their nature and Communion from the Holy Mysteries merely because they are children.

8.28.0.en: They went down both into the water: Philip and the eunuch went down from the chariot to the pool of water that was beside the desert road, and the man was baptized by the hand of Philip.

8.29.0.en: Were come up: this shows that it was a collection of water into which the eunuch went down and immersed, and so was baptized by the hand of Philip. Caught away: the Holy Spirit suddenly transported him from this place to the city of Azotus to complete his work of preaching in it.

8.29.1.en: Rejoicing: in his faith and his Baptism, longing to preach this faith to his country.

8.29.2.en: The Holy Spirit transported Philip to the city of Azotus, so the minister no longer saw him, but went on his way rejoicing in his new faith.

8.30.0.en: Azotus: a Palestinian city lying north of Gaza at a distance of 24 miles.

8.30.1.en: Caesarea: named after Caesar, it is a great city on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea south of Acre.

8.30.2.en: Philip began to resume the preaching in the Palestinian city of Azotus until he reached Caesarea, from which afterward came the father of church history, the historian Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea, and in which a theological school was founded with scholars represented by the scholar Origen, who founded this school after he moved to it from Alexandria, and which was the dwelling place of Philip the deacon and his virgin daughters who prophesied (ch. 21:8, 9). Such was the activity of the first Church, which was restless in its work, but always moved to complete the mission under the guidance of the Holy Spirit and in obedience to Him.

8.30.3.en: May we move to serve God, and come out of our many occupations so that we may draw souls to enjoy fellowship with Him in the Church.

8.30.4.en: The conversion of Paul and the miracles of Peter

9.0.0.en: Breathing out threatenings: threatening and menacing, with his mouth uttering evil words full of hatred and vengeance. After the killing of Stephen, Saul was still very zealous for the destruction of Christianity, so he was threatening and killing many, trying to obtain from the high priest sentences of death against the Christians, who were called disciples.

9.1.0.en: Damascus: an ancient city lying north of Jerusalem at a distance of about 280 km, that is, a seven days' journey from it.

9.1.1.en: The synagogues: the communities of Jews present in no small number in Damascus.

9.1.2.en: The Way: the followers of the way of Christ, for so the Christians were called in the apostolic age, and he expected some of them to be in Damascus, of those who had been scattered by the Jewish persecution in Jerusalem.

9.1.3.en: Women: his cruelty appears in that he binds and drives not only men but women also. Saul asked the high priest to give him letters to the governor of Damascus and the elders of the Jewish communities, who had a large colony in Damascus, so that he might seize the Christians, men or women, with full force and transfer them in chains to be tried and tortured in Jerusalem.

9.2.0.en: While Paul was on the road near Damascus at noon (ch. 26:13), a heavenly light suddenly flashed around him, brighter than the light of the noonday sun.

9.3.0.en: In his great terror, he fell to the ground and saw the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, who spoke with him rebuking him and warning him of his persecution of the Christians, which Christ regarded as persecution of Himself personally. His rebuke of him was in humility and gentleness, as though asking the reason for that persecution, for the Lord and His Church are in union like the head and the body. The speech was in the Hebrew language, and those with him did not understand the words although they heard the voice (ch. 26:14).

9.4.0.en: Pricks: plural of goad, which is an iron needle that the farmer uses to prick the animal so that it hurries on its way and work.

9.4.1.en: Saul asked who was speaking, and God made clear to him that He is Jesus, which is His name according to the flesh, to make clear to him that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and in compassion for him made him understand that he would harm no one but himself, because all the sorrows of the Church are turned into blessings and joys and the harm falls on its persecutors and not on it, like one who kicks with his foot iron needles, which are the goads, so his foot is wounded and the blood flows from it, while the goads suffer no harm.

9.5.0.en: Saul was greatly bewildered because he was surprised by a divine proclamation of the divinity of Jesus, and was terrified when he sensed the greatness of the wrong he had been committing during his persecution of the Church, and in submission he asked for God's counsel in order to carry it out, so God directed him to enter Damascus, where he would be told what was required of him.

9.5.1.en: Thus God made clear the necessity of submitting to the Church and her priests, to receive the Holy Sacraments from their hand and to hear the teachings and guidance, for a man cannot be content with his personal relationship with God apart from the Church, or with hearing the voice of God and the guidance of the Spirit without the guidance of the Church.

9.6.0.en: All who were with him were silent with terror, not understanding the words although they heard the voice, and they did not see the person of the Lord but saw only the light.

9.7.0.en: He saw no man: because he had seen Christ in His strong light, whereas those with him saw something of the light and did not see Christ, so they did not lose their sight. This was by God's permission that he might be humbled, for humility is the entrance to the spiritual life.

9.7.1.en: Saul arose after losing his sight temporarily from the intensity of the light, so he could no longer see anyone. Thus for one who sees the Lord, the sight of anyone else becomes small. They led him by the hand, and he entered Damascus not in the manner he had wanted, not in a grand procession but in humility and reverence.

9.8.0.en: Saul remained for three days in fasting, constant prayers and meditation on what had happened, seeing nothing throughout this time.

9.8.1.en: So the Lord intervenes in His love in our lives to change our course at the right moment, and therefore we must be discerning of His voice and obedient to Him.

9.9.s.en: (2) Faith, Baptism and the beginning of ministry

9.9.0.en: A disciple: that is, a Christian.

9.9.1.en: A vision: a sight he saw while awake and not in a dream.

9.9.2.en: Of Tarsus: from Tarsus, the capital of Cilicia in Asia Minor (present-day Turkey), a great city famous for learning.

9.9.3.en: He prayeth: his prayers now are in humility and different from his former prayers as a Pharisee in pride.

9.9.4.en: He hath seen in a vision: Saul was awake, and although he could not see the material things around him, God revealed to him a spiritual sight, which was that a priest named Ananias entered to him and put his hands on his eyes and he saw. The Lord appeared to one of the Christians of Damascus, whose name was Ananias, and he was a priest because he baptized Saul afterward, and the Lord said to him in the vision to go to the main street in Damascus, which was called Straight Street, and was the longest street in the city, running from east to west, four meters wide and lined by rows of columns, and it still exists today. And He asked him to go to the house of a man named Judas, where he would find Saul of Tarsus praying, and the Lord informed him that Saul had seen him, that is, had seen Ananias in a vision, putting his hands on Saul's eyes so that he might see. Thus God gave clear signs to Ananias and to Saul to reassure them.

9.10.0.en: Ananias was bewildered when he heard God's words in the vision about going to Saul, because he had heard from the Christians of Jerusalem who had fled to Damascus of Saul's wickedness and his persecution of the believers, and that he had come to Damascus with authority from the high priest to seize the Christians, torture them and kill them, but in spite of that he was ready to obey God, for he declared his submission at the beginning of the vision by saying, "Behold, I am here, Lord."

9.11.0.en: Gentiles: he will preach to non-Jews, and this was something far from the understanding of the Jews, for they thought that they alone were the people of God, and none other would believe in the Messiah.

9.11.1.en: Kings: he means the rulers, of kings and governors, who tried the Apostle Paul, and he even preached Christ to some of them, such as Felix, Festus, Agrippa and Nero.

9.11.2.en: The children of Israel: Paul preached, at the beginning of his entering any country, to the Jews first and then to the Gentiles in it. God reassured Ananias to go to Paul, since He had chosen him as a vessel to fill, to proclaim His name to many Gentiles and kings and to the people of the children of Israel; a thing that was perfectly fulfilled in Paul's preaching in the future, and He also informed him that he would suffer much for the sake of Christ, and that is something every Christian goes through.

9.12.0.en: Ananias was reassured and went to the house of Judas, and blessed Saul by putting his hands on him for blessing and not for ordination, and called him brother in gentleness and love despite all he had done before, and told him that Christ had sent him to him after appearing to him on the road to Damascus, to restore to him sight and insight by faith and to be filled with the Holy Spirit after Baptism.

9.13.0.en: Scales fell from Saul's eyes to confirm God's miracle, and these scales are a symbol of the sin that had veiled Christ from him, so he received sight immediately and Ananias baptized him.

9.14.0.en: Saul took food and was strengthened after his fast of three days, and stayed some days with the Christians of Damascus. Thus the wolf was turned into a lamb.

9.15.1.en: He preached: his preaching includes that after his Baptism and also after his return from his retreat in the Arabian desert. The synagogues: the Apostles used to enter them as Jews and then preach Christ, confirming their words from the prophecies of the prophets.

9.15.2.en: The Church began her ministry as a daughter of the Jewish nation and emerging from it, which helped the spread of Christianity among the Jews. And Saul began to preach in the synagogues of the Jews in the name of Christ and His divinity; but we must know that after his Baptism he went to the Arabian desert bordering Damascus, where he stayed three years in retreat in which Christ appeared to him, and delivered to him the faith and the Holy Sacraments (Gal 1:16-18), so some of the Fathers call him the thirteenth of the Apostles, and then he returned to Damascus for ministry.

9.16.0.en: Saul's ministry was met with great astonishment by the Jews, who knew his past in Jerusalem in opposing the Christians, whom he had now joined, having come to torture them.

9.17.0.en: The Jews wondered greatly at his power of persuasion as a student of the Law and the Prophets, proving that Jesus is the Christ.

9.17.1.en: Truly nothing is too hard for the Lord!.. Who would have thought that such a complete change would happen?!

9.17.2.en: He who changed Saul, which means (the asked-for one), into Paul, which means (the little one), still asks us to allow Him to change our lives into true children of His.

9.17.3.en: God is able to change you whatever your sins or weaknesses, for He is your Creator who loves you and is able to do all things, but it remains that you do not reject the voice of God within you or when you hear it from the Church and her servants. Do not resist the word of God or wallow in your sins, but rise up, confident of His support for you, and you will gain your life and become great like Paul.

9.18.0.en: After Saul completed three years in the desert called Arabia, he returned to Damascus, and the Jews were greatly distressed by his preaching, so they took counsel to kill him as they had done with Stephen.

9.19.0.en: Saul learned of their plot, for the Jews had agreed with the governor of the city to seize him, so they watched the gates of the city to seize him when he came out of one of them.

9.20.0.en: The believers, the disciples of Christ, took him to the house of one of them that adjoined the wall of the city, where they let him down from it in a large basket so that he could get out without the Jews seeing him. The decision was based on Christ's words to His disciples: "When they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another" (Mt 10:23), so that the preaching might spread.

9.20.1.en: Thus Paul escaped from the plot of the Jews and left Damascus as a fugitive, contrary to what he had expected when he came to the city to seize the Christians in it and go out in pride dragging many of them to be tortured and killed in Jerusalem.

9.21.0.en: Saul arrived from Damascus in Jerusalem and tried to join the Christians there, but they were afraid of him, thinking he was a spy for the Jews, especially because of the long period of his disappearance in the Arabian desert, which made them suspect that he had returned to his Judaism.

9.22.0.en: Barnabas: one of the first disciples who followed Christ with the twelve, and he was rich and sold his field and gave it to the Apostles for the needs of the believers (Acts 4:36, 37). He was of the tribe of Levi and had lived before in Cyprus, so he was Cypriot by nationality.

9.22.1.en: Barnabas intervened and brought him to Peter and James (Gal 1:18, 19), the two Apostles who were still in Jerusalem, because the rest were traveling to preach, and told them of the sincerity of his faith and Christ's appearing to him on the road to Damascus and his ministry in it.

9.23.0.en: At last the Christians of Jerusalem were reassured about him, and he began his preaching there, but for about fifteen days only (Gal 1:18).

9.24.0.en: Saul began to persuade the Greek-speaking Jews in the synagogues where Stephen had addressed them, so they also tried to kill him, and the Christians sent him to the city of Caesarea, which lies between Acre and Joppa, and God had also commanded him to leave Jerusalem (ch. 22:17-21), and then he traveled from Caesarea to Tarsus by sea and stayed there about three or four years.

9.24.1.en: Be strong in proclaiming the truth however much others oppose you or you are exposed to trouble, confident that God keeps you to proclaim His name, and at the same time do not waste your time in clashing with others but flee from evil to continue your positive work in calling everyone to life with God.

9.25.0.en: Had rest: the Jewish persecution of the Church subsided because many Christians had been scattered in the countries of the world and left Jerusalem, in addition to the change of the greatest opponent of the Christians, Saul of Tarsus, who became a Christian and a preacher of Christ, and finally because the Jews were occupied with the conflict with the Roman authority.

9.25.1.en: The fear of the Lord: it gave the believers piety and a spiritual walk, which drew many to faith.

9.25.2.en: The comfort of the Holy Ghost: that is, His encouragements and His support for the children of God.

9.25.3.en: The Church extended from Jerusalem to Judea and then Samaria and Galilee, that is, all the parts of the land of the Jews; and the Jews' persecution of the Christians subsided after their killing of Stephen, because the Jews were occupied with their problems with the Emperor "Caligula," who ordered that a statue of himself be set up in the Temple, so the whole country was in uproar and the governor advised him to postpone this matter. Thus the Jews forgot the Church in the midst of their problems, and the Church grew and multiplied in the fear of God and the comfort of the Comforter Spirit.

9.26.0.en: Lydda: a city lying east of Joppa at a distance of 9 miles.

9.26.1.en: The Apostle Peter began a visiting tour, and came down to the believers at Lydda. We note that he was visiting only those who had turned to Christianity from the Jews, because the faith had not yet spread among the Gentiles. We see here a new name for the Christians, who were called first disciples, then believers, then saints, then brethren and finally Christians.

9.27.0.en: There was in Lydda a Christian, sick with paralysis for eight years and known to all, named Aeneas, and Peter healed him in the name of Jesus Christ and commanded him to rise and make his bed himself, and he arose immediately.

9.28.0.en: Sharon: it is the fertile plain extending from Joppa to Caesarea.

9.28.1.en: All who dwelt at Lydda and Sharon, of the believers, saw him, and the miracle was a cause of the strengthening of their faith.

9.28.2.en: "To every purpose under heaven there is a time" (Eccl 3:1), and the Lord is able to stretch out the hand of healing at the right time. So let us not despair if the trial or illness is prolonged, but let us benefit from it in strengthening our relationship with God, confident of His power and wisdom, which chooses the right time.

9.29.0.en: Joppa: a port on the Mediterranean Sea thirty miles south of Caesarea and 45 miles west of Jerusalem, and it is the most important port in Judea.

9.29.2.en: There lived at Joppa a Christian woman named Tabitha, which is a Syriac name meaning gazelle, and she was righteous and charitable.

9.30.0.en: Tabitha fell sick and died, and they washed her, for it is the custom of Christians to wash the body after death (as a symbol of purity and cleanness, but it is merely a custom and not a necessary thing), and they did not bury her but sent two men to call Peter from Lydda to Joppa (15 km) to attend the funeral and console the believers, and asked him to come quickly so that the burial would not be delayed. Perhaps they had hope of her being raised from the dead.

9.31.0.en: Peter came quickly and went up with those gathered to the upper room where the body was, and the widows showed him, weeping, the garments that Tabitha used to make for the brethren of the Lord, and Peter was deeply moved.

9.32.0.en: Sat up: a proclamation of her life after having been dead.

9.32.1.en: Gave her his hand: so that she would be sure that she was alive and lean on his hand and rise and go out to those gathered. The saints: the believers sanctified in Christ.

9.32.2.en: Peter put everyone out of the room so that he might pray to the Lord to raise her, so that no one would see him doing that, because he does not seek fame or greatness, and he asked Christ to raise her and she sat up at once and He restored her alive.

9.33.0.en: Tarried: he settled in Joppa to complete his preaching of Christ.

9.33.2.en: After that Peter stayed a long time in Joppa in the house of Simon the tanner.

9.33.3.en: Truly "almsgiving delivers from death," as the Scripture says (Tob 4:7). May you love giving because it is a great blessing, and know that when you give to one in need you are offering love to Christ Himself. So do not be lax in helping all those around you even by a small deed or kind words, and if you are unable to act and speak, your prayer moves God's mercies, so that He cares for them.

9.33.4.en: The acceptance of the Gentiles into the faith
